title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 2: Judicial Reform Is Also the Business of Business
keywords: Judicial Reform Is Also the Business of Business
Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's address to the Management Association of the Philippines arguing that because good governance and economic stability require predictable, speedy and objective justice, 'judicial reform becomes also the business of business.'

A diagnosis of the three most common complaints against the judiciary -- corruption, incompetence and delay, or CID -- introduced through three apocryphal incidents in the life of the fictional 'Hukom Juan Suplado' and backed by a World Bank report and Social Weather Stations survey figures.

A survey of the Supreme Court's reform program under its Centenary Executive Committee: upgrading law schools, reforming the recruitment of magistrates, rationalizing judicial compensation, improving the disciplinary process, modernizing judicial tools and facilities, and easing the judicial environment.

Four concrete things the business community can do -- refuse every corrupt shortcut, fund private-sector reform efforts, encourage competent and ethical lawyers to join the bench, and pray for the judiciary -- closing with Bishop Benny Tudtud's prayer 'Disturb Us O Lord.'
sub_topics: He opens personally, thanking Ric Pascua of MAP, whom he met in Hong Kong through the charismatic community Bukas Loob sa Diyos, and praising not his houses, cars or golf memberships but what money could not buy -- a happy marriage, family, self-reliance and faith in God.

He greets MAP president Johnny Santos, chosen 'Management Man of the Year 1994' over two well-known tycoons because he had made management the career center of his life rather than a means to entrepreneurial gain.

He apologizes for having withdrawn from his business and professional circles since joining the Court, explaining that justices are 'entombed in judicial cloisters' and that jurists must not only be impartial but appear so.
He announces his three topics: the main complaints against the judiciary, the reforms that would address them, and what the business community can do to help.

The three Hukom Juan Suplado stories -- the lawyer 'selling' a Mercedes Benz for one thousand pesos, the mistranslated cross-examination, and the 75-year-old man who turns out to be the infant the two women had fought over -- illustrating corruption, incompetence and delay.

Corruption is not only direct bribery but 'the three ships' of friendship, relationship and kinship; the World Bank's 'Combating Corruption in the Philippines' and a February 2000 SWS survey report 62 percent believing in significant judicial corruption, 65 percent that many lawyers could be bribed and 57 percent the same of judges.

Incompetence 'ranges from poor command of language to utter lack of knowledge of elementary law,' while delay flows from antiquated procedures and from even the best rules being misused to confuse, outwit or bankrupt opponents.

Reform one -- upgrading law schools: a Committee on Legal Education, a new law transferring supervision from CHED to the Board of Legal Education, the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education organized by Attys. Ricardo J. Romulo and Arthur Lim, and a Study Group on Bar Reforms.

Reform two -- recruitment: appointments only from the Judicial and Bar Council's list, now further restricted by RA 8557's pre-judicature course requirement, with Philja providing continuing education and needing P500 million for its three-hectare Tagaytay plant.

Reform three -- compensation: about a third of trial court positions vacant, RTC judges paid P24,127 a month and Supreme Court justices P38,500 while new Makati associates earn more; the judiciary needs real fiscal independence and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, given a budget of P6.28 billion against a national budget over P665 billion.

Reform four -- discipline: more than forty judges dismissed in two years and twice that number suspended or fined, yet an unduly long process treats frivolous and meritorious complaints alike and blocks promotion and retirement while a complaint pends.

Judicial tools and facilities: decent Halls of Justice to replace 'squalid, unsanitary and sometimes subhuman courtrooms,' 1,500 computers with Supreme Court decisions from 1901 encoded, and the Internet homepage www.supremecourt.gov.ph.

Judicial management: 25,000 personnel supervised through the Office of the Court Administrator, which is usually headed by jurists although 'eminent jurists do not necessarily make excellent administrators' -- hence his call to make judicial administration a career in itself.

Reforms in the judicial environment: encouraging ADR, requiring courts to explore discovery before trial, finding alternatives to the flood of BP 22 cases that turn courts into a collection agency, and filtering capital appeals through the Court of Appeals.

First thing business can do: never agree to corrupt or less-than-honest methods, disbelieve lawyers who ask money to line magistrates' pockets, and remember that 'corruption will take place only if litigants abet or consent to it.'

Second: support private-sector reform efforts -- the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education (P10 million from the Court, P10 million from lawyers and P30 million to be raised from clients), Bantay Katarungan of Salonga and Ordoñez, and Justice Feria's Foundation for Judicial Excellence.

Third: encourage competent and ethical lawyers to join the judiciary and restore balance in appointments, noting that of the six private-sector appointees among the fifteen justices when he joined in 1995, only he and Justice Vitug remain.

Fourth: pray for the judiciary -- even those satisfied with its performance -- so that it does not rest on its laurels, since 'reforming society and its imperfections is never complete'; he closes with Bishop Benny Tudtud's prayer 'Disturb Us O Lord' and 'Maraming salamat po.'

stances.claim: The three most common complaints against the judiciary are corruption, incompetence and delay -- CID -- and corruption includes not only bribery but the 'three ships' of friendship, relationship and kinship.
stances.rhetorical_move: humor-as-diagnosis: three apocryphal Hukom Juan Suplado stories decoded into three institutional failings, then corroborated by survey data

stances.claim: Because good governance and economic stability require predictable, speedy and objective justice, judicial reform is also the business of business, and MAP members have a direct stake in eliminating CID.
stances.rhetorical_move: audience-stake framing that converts a judicial problem into a business problem

stances.claim: Corruption in the courts will occur only if litigants abet or consent to it, so businessmen must refuse every corrupt shortcut and never believe lawyers who ask money to line magistrates' pockets.
stances.rhetorical_move: demand-side argument placing responsibility on the payer while defending the integrity of most judges

stances.claim: Judicial compensation must be rationalized through real fiscal independence and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, since a third of trial court posts are vacant and new Makati associates outearn Supreme Court justices.
stances.rhetorical_move: salary comparison with the audience's own firms, followed by a structural budget proposal

stances.claim: Appointments to the appellate courts have tilted too far toward career jurists, and a proper balance requires appointing outstanding members of the bar and the academe directly so that novel ideas and fresh blood enter judicial circulation.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-observation argument using the shrinking count of private-sector justices as evidence

stances.claim: Reform is never finished, so even those satisfied with the judiciary should pray that it not grow complacent with minuscule success or satisfied with adulation.

notable_anecdotes: He recalls meeting Ric Pascua and his wife Rizza in Hong Kong more than ten years earlier, not through the First Pacific Group but through the Catholic charismatic community Bukas Loob sa Diyos.
He recounts how Johnny Santos won Management Man of the Year 1994 over two well-known tycoons because he had made management the career center of his life.
He apologizes to old friends for refusing visitors and telephone calls since his appointment, explaining that justices are 'entombed in judicial cloisters.'
The Mercedes Benz joke: a lawyer offers to sell the judge a new car for one thousand pesos, and Hukom Suplado answers, 'I will buy two!'
The mistranslation joke, in which both the interpreter and the judge garble the Tagalog for 'what did you see' into words meaning sawing and sewing.
The Solomon-like custody case in which a frail 75-year-old man limps to the bench to announce that the two women are dead and that he was the baby they were fighting over.
He notes that of the six justices appointed directly from the private sector when he joined in 1995, only he and Justice Jose C. Vitug remain.
He ends the address with Bishop Benny Tudtud's prayer 'Disturb Us O Lord' and the Filipino closing 'Maraming salamat po.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' is Panganiban's address to the Management Association of the Philippines, opening with personal tributes to MAP's Ric Pascua and Johnny Santos and an apology to old friends for the seclusion of a justice 'entombed in judicial cloisters,' since jurists must not only be impartial but appear so. He then poses three questions: the main complaints against the judiciary, the reforms that answer them, and what business can do. Through three apocryphal stories about 'Hukom Juan Suplado' -- a lawyer offering to sell the judge a Mercedes for a thousand pesos, a garbled court translation, and a 75-year-old man who turns out to be the infant two women once fought over -- he identifies corruption, incompetence and delay, or CID. Corruption, he says, includes the 'three ships' of friendship, relationship and kinship, and he cites the World Bank's 'Combating Corruption in the Philippines' and a February 2000 SWS survey in which 62 percent perceived significant judicial corruption. He then surveys the Court's reform program under its Centenary Executive Committee: upgrading law schools through a Committee on Legal Education, the new Board of Legal Education and the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education; reforming recruitment through the JBC and RA 8557's pre-judicature course; rationalizing compensation through fiscal independence and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law; improving the disciplinary process; building Halls of Justice, distributing 1,500 computers and opening the Court's website; professionalizing judicial administration; and easing dockets through ADR, discovery, alternatives to BP 22 cases and filtered capital appeals. Because stability requires predictable justice, 'judicial reform becomes also the business of business,' and he asks four things: never bribe a judge, fund private reform efforts, send good lawyers to the bench, and pray -- closing with Bishop Benny Tudtud's 'Disturb Us O Lord.'
